newsitem.title: USA: New fund offers best of the best.
newsitem.headline: New fund offers best of the best.

text.p: What's the biggest problem facing mutual funds today? How about success.

The enormous growth of the mutual fund industry has led to huge asset growth for many funds. At the same time, the cult of performance has caused investors to plough money into the funds that have achieved the best returns in recent years.

When that happens, the performance of those funds often suffers. For example, after Warburg Pincus Emerging Growth jumped 46.2 percent in 1995, its assets more than doubled. Last year, however, the fund returned only 9.9 percent, compared with a 14.8 percent return for the Russell 2000 Index and 20.3 percent for the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks.
One problem: when funds' assets balloon, the managers often don't have enough good ideas to invest all the money that's coming their way.
A fund launched on Jan. 6 aims to solve that problem. If it does, you can expect it to inspire many imitators in the coming months and years.

The fund, Masters Select Equity (800-656-8864; $5,000 minimum investment; no-load), is the brainchild of Ken Gregory and Craig Litman of L/G Research, which publishes "No-Load Fund Analyst" newsletter.

During the past decade, the pair has impressed investors by publishing thoughtful analyses of market trends and specific funds. Their newsletter monitors a select group of funds -- about 100 in all -- whose managers have proven themselves among the best in the industry. Often, the No-Load Fund Analyst is peppered with manager interviews that offer insight into what some of the sharpest minds in the business are thinking.

The new fund is designed to invest in the best ideas of six world-class fund managers, who will work independently to choose their favourite stocks -- between five and 15 names apiece -- for the portfolio.

"We're trying to isolate the stockpickers' skills in a way that traditional funds can't do," says Gregory. "Most stockpickers usually own a handful of favourite stocks at any given time, which tend to outperform the other stocks in their portfolios."
The managers of Masters' Select Equity include six names that are familiar to seasoned fund investors, and cover a range of investment styles and equity categories.
The six are:

-- Shelby Davis, whose Selected American Shares has climbed 20.4 percent annually during the past three years, while taking only about 90 percent as much risk as the typical equity fund. Davis made his name running the Davis New York Venture Fund, which has gained 14.4 percent annually since 1969.

-- Jean Marie Eveillard, manager of SoGen Overseas and SoGen International, who will look for undervalued shares in overseas markets. Eveillard's eclectic, low-risk, contrarian approach has delivered 15.8 percent annual returns at his flagship International Fund since 1982. What's more, the fund has been only about half as volatile as its average competitor during the past decade.

-- Mason Hawkins buys shares of large and mid-sized companies when they are out-of-favour or neglected. His value approach has delivered 15.8 percent annual returns at Longleaf Partners since 1987, at below-average risk.

-- Spiros Segalas, manager of Harbour Capital Appreciation, buys shares of large companies with rising earnings. His fund has gained 16.1 percent annually during the past five years versus 15.2 percent for the S&P 500.

-- Foster Friess and his team at Brandywine Fund have led the fund to a 19 percent annual return since its inception in 1985. They hold small and mid-sized company shares with strong earnings momentum.

-- Dick Weiss, one of the top small-company stockpickers in the industry, has delivered 19.1 percent annual returns at Strong Common Stock since 1992. He favours small growth companies when their shares are trading at bargain prices relative to earnings potential and other factors.
With a line-up like that, investors might expect the fund to top the mutual fund rankings a year from now. But don't count on it, Gregory warns.

"The diversification among different categories and stocks will smooth out its performance and keep it off the top of the charts," he says. "But over a full market cycle, we believe that it will deliver superior performance."
Seems like a reasonable bet. But the fund will fluctuate with the stock market, and as with any new fund there's the potential for unforeseen pitfalls -- so don't bet your entire savings just yet.

Instead, consider a modest investment for now and watch what happens. If the idea behind the fund proves as sound in practice as it seems in theory, you may have a good equity fund to anchor your long-term portfolio.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
